_meta.schema: list of {cve, name, pattern, case_insensitive, category, why_specific, reference}
_meta.curation: hand-written from public CVE write-ups; never generated or scraped
admission_bar: A match here returns Malicious on its own — the only single-source Malicious in the module (docs/waf_payload_analyzer.md D10). Every other path requires two independent layers.
That exception is only defensible while every pattern is impossible in legitimate traffic. 'Well known CVE' is NOT sufficient grounds for an entry; 'this string has no benign reason to exist' is.

why_specific is mandatory and must state why benign traffic cannot produce the pattern. An entry whose justification is only 'this is a famous exploit' invalidates the exception for every other entry in the file.
Grow deliberately, based on what is actually seen (briefing 10). A larger set is not a better set.

rejected.reason: Proposed by the source briefing, and it matches ordinary Outlook Web Access traffic — OWA serves its own scripts from /owa/auth/. Shipping it would mark every Exchange user's browser as a confirmed exploit, at Malicious, from a single source. The autodiscover SSRF pattern below is used instead.
The distinctive marker is an HTTP header, and this module only ever sees a path and a payload. A path-only approximation would match benign /ecp/ traffic.

fingerprints.name: Log4Shell
fingerprints.why_specific: A JNDI lookup expression inside a ${} interpolation, naming a remote protocol. No application legitimately asks a user to supply one; the nested-${} alternative covers the ${${lower:j}ndi:} obfuscation used to bypass early filters.

fingerprints.name: Spring4Shell
fingerprints.why_specific: Reaches the JVM ClassLoader through Spring's data-binding property path. A legitimate form never binds a parameter named class.module.classLoader — the property chain exists only to escape the bound object.

fingerprints.name: ProxyShell
fingerprints.why_specific: The Exchange autodiscover SSRF: a query string beginning with @ so the explicit-path parser mis-routes the request to the backend. Ordinary autodiscover requests carry an Email parameter, never a leading @ in the query. The leading slash is not required and the ? may arrive percent-encoded, because the exploit is commonly seen nested inside another parameter.

fingerprints.name: Shellshock
fingerprints.why_specific: An empty Bash function definition immediately followed by a command separator — the exact byte sequence that triggers the parser bug. It is not valid or meaningful content in any user-supplied field.

fingerprints.name: Struts2 S2-045
fingerprints.why_specific: OGNL expressions that reach Struts internals and disable its member-access sandbox. Both are framework-internal names that no client-supplied value has a reason to contain.

fingerprints.name: Apache 2.4.49 path traversal
fingerprints.why_specific: Traversal that encodes only one of the two dots, which is what slipped past the 2.4.49 path check. The mixed literal-and-encoded form has no legitimate use: a real relative path is either percent-encoded or it is not, never half of each within a single segment.

fingerprints.name: Pulse Secure arbitrary file read
fingerprints.why_specific: Traversal out of the Pulse Secure web root to an internal endpoint. The literal ../ between two product-specific path segments cannot be produced by normal navigation.

fingerprints.name: F5 BIG-IP TMUI RCE
fingerprints.why_specific: A traversal appended to the TMUI login page, and the unauthenticated hsqldb endpoint it reaches. Neither shape occurs when the interface is used normally.
